facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus lived during the Middle Eocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Eocene,

facts.statement: The genus Dentaneosuchus was described by Martin and colleagues in 2023.
facts.quote: authority: Martin et al., 2023

facts.statement: The type species of Dentaneosuchus is Atacisaurus crassiproratus.
facts.quote: type_species: Atacisaurus crassiproratus

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus was previously known as Atacisaurus crassiproratus and Iberosuchus crassiproratus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Atacisaurus crassiproratus Astre, 1931 Iberosuchus crassiproratus (Godinot et al., 2018)

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus fossils have been found in Issel and Réalmont in France.
facts.quote: Dentaneosuchus is a genus of large bodied sebecid crocodylomorph from the Middle Eocene of Issel and Réalmont (France).

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus was the largest terrestrial carnivore of Cenozoic Europe.
facts.quote: It reached a similar size to the enormous Barinasuchus, making it not only one of the biggest sebecids but also the biggest terrestrial carnivore of Cenozoic Europe.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus was an apex predator capable of hunting large prey like Lophiodon.
facts.quote: Dentaneosuchus would have been an apex predator of its environment, capable of taking large prey such as Lophiodon.

facts.statement: The first fossil of Dentaneosuchus was discovered in the Sables du Castrais Formation near Issel, France, and originally named Atacisaurus crassiproratus by Gaston Astre in 1931.
facts.quote: The first fossil of Dentaneosuchus, a mandibular symphysis catalogued as specimen MHNT.PAL.2006.0.53., was discovered in the Sables du Castrais Formation near Issel in southern France and assigned to the genus Atacisaurus by Gaston Astre in 1931, creating the name Atacisaurus crassiproratus.

facts.statement: In 2018, Godinot and colleagues reclassified the species as Iberosuchus crassiproratus.
facts.quote: In 2018 Godinot and colleagues went as far as to fully place the specimen in Iberosuchus while retaining the species name, creating the new combination Iberosuchus crassiproratus.

facts.statement: Additional sebecid specimens were discovered near Réalmont, France, in 1997.
facts.quote: Excavations in France meanwhile continued to yield sebecid material, including specimens discovered in 1997 near Réalmont.

facts.statement: Martin and colleagues distinguished Dentaneosuchus from Iberosuchus macrodon based on mandibular remains from two different localities.
facts.quote: Martin et al. compared the Réalmont material with both Iberosuchus and the Issel symphysis, determining that there were no differences between the mandibular remains from the two localities yet clear deviations from Iberosuchus macrodon.

facts.statement: The name Dentaneosuchus combines Latin and Greek roots meaning "showing teeth" and "crocodile".
facts.quote: The name Dentaneosuchus derives from the Latin "dentaneo", which roughly translates to "showing teeth" or "frightfull" in allusion to its hypothesized role as apex predator, and the Greek "souchos" meaning crocodile, derived from the name of the Egyption deity Sobek.

facts.statement: The skull of Dentaneosuchus was altirostral, meaning it was higher than it was wide.
facts.quote: The skull of Dentaneosuchus was altirostral, meaning that unlike in modern crocodilians, it was higher than it was wide.

facts.statement: The premaxilla of Dentaneosuchus contained five teeth on each side.
facts.quote: The premaxilla contains five teeth on either side, with the bone bulging around the roots of tooth.

facts.statement: The fourth premaxillary tooth of Dentaneosuchus was twice the size of the second tooth.
facts.quote: The first premaxillary tooth, located close to the midline, is the smallest and the teeth get progressively larger until reaching their maximum size at the fourth tooth, which is twice the size of the second.

facts.statement: The maxilla and nasal bone of Dentaneosuchus were fused together.
facts.quote: The maxilla appears to be fused to the nasal bone, obscuring the suture between the two.

facts.statement: The nasal bone of Dentaneosuchus was long and stretched from the front of the rostrum to the frontal bone.
facts.quote: The nasal was long, stretching from the front of the rostrum where it contacts the premaxilla and likely contributed to the bony wall separating the nares to the frontal bone.

facts.statement: The prefrontal bones of Dentaneosuchus were plate-like and overhung the eye sockets.
facts.quote: The prefrontals are plate-like bones situated atop the head and overhanging the eye sockets.

facts.statement: At least 19 teeth were present in the mandible of Dentaneosuchus.
facts.quote: A total of at least 19 teeth is thought to have been present in the mandible of Dentaneosuchus.

facts.statement: The teeth of Dentaneosuchus were ziphodont with fine serrations on their carinae.
facts.quote: The teeth of Dentaneosuchus are generally robust thanks to the nearly circular tooth roots, they are still truly ziphodont, with slight compression and carinae covered in fine serrations.

facts.statement: The presence of sebecids in Europe, far from their primary range in South America, remains not entirely resolved.
facts.quote: Because of this Dentaneosuchus could play an important part in deciphering the origins and dispersal of European sebecids, as their presence on the continent, far away from their primary range in South America, is still not entirely resolved.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus was tentatively recovered as the most basal member of the family Sebecidae.
facts.quote: It was tentatively recovered as the basalmost member of the family Sebecidae.

facts.statement: It is debated why crocodylomorphs lost their position as top predators in Europe by the end of the Eocene.
facts.quote: However, for as of yet unknown reasons crocodylomorphs would lose their spot as top predator in this part of the world by the end of the Eocene, with Dentaneosuchus representing one of the last members of its group in Europe.

facts.statement: Four osteoderms have been discovered in Dentaneosuchus, but their exact location on the body is uncertain because no sebecid preserves articulated armor.
facts.quote: Four osteoderms have been discovered, but as no sebecid preserves articulated armor it is not certain where on the body they would have been located.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus osteoderms included a larger sub-trapezoid type and a smaller ovoid type that was longer than it was wide.
facts.quote: The larger type is sub-trapezoid, while the smaller osteoderm variety is ovoid and longer than wide.

facts.statement: The osteoderms of Dentaneosuchus resemble those of Baurusuchus but are sufficiently distinct to be different.
facts.quote: Both bear some resemblance to those of Baurusuchus, but are sufficiently distinct.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus is considered the largest terrestrial predator of Cenozoic Europe.
facts.quote: Regardless of the specifics, this renders Dentaneosuchus the largest terrestrial predator of Cenozoic Europe.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Dentaneosuchus in the family Sebecidae, closely related to the South American Baurusuchidae within the group Sebecosuchia.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analysis conducted on the material of Dentaneosuchus places it in the family Sebecidae, which was recovered as closely related to the South American Baurusuchidae with which it forms Sebecosuchia.

facts.statement: Within Sebecidae, Dentaneosuchus was recovered as having affinities with the German genus Bergisuchus.
facts.quote: Within Sebecidae, Dentaneosuchus was recovered as having affinities with the German Bergisuchus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that differences between Dentaneosuchus and Bergisuchus might change with age, but conclude it is premature to make conclusive statements on the implications.
facts.quote: While Martin and colleagues raise the possibility that some of the difference between the two could change with age, they conclude that it would be premature to make any conclusive statements on what this may imply.

facts.statement: Authors note that many unknowns regarding Dentaneosuchus anatomy could greatly impact its phylogenetic placement and that future discoveries could change its position drastically.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the authors also point out that there are still many unknowns regarding the anatomy of Dentaneosuchus that would greatly impact its phylogenetic placement and how future discoveries could change its position drastically.

facts.statement: A 2025 study recovered broadly similar phylogenetic results, featuring a close relationship between the European taxa Bergisuchus and Iberosuchus.
facts.quote: A later study from 2025 recovered broadly similar results, featuring the same close relationship between the European taxa Bergisuchus and Iberosuchus.

facts.statement: The range of Dentaneosuchus is currently confined to the Bartonian stage of the Eocene.
facts.quote: For this reason, the range of Dentaneosuchus is currently confined to the Bartonian stage of the Eocene.

facts.statement: Some localities previously associated with Dentaneosuchus were placed in the MP13-14 biozones (Lutetian), an age similar to the Spanish Duero Basin and much older than the Réalmont locality in France.
facts.quote: The pre-Bartonian age was later corroborated by Badiola & Cuesta (2008), who place it firmly within the MP13-14 biozones (Lutetian), a similar age as the Spanish Duero Basin and much older than the locality of Réalmont in France.

facts.statement: The origins of European sebecids are a debated subject due to a poor fossil record outside of South America.
facts.quote: The origins of European sebecids remains a debated subject and is shrouded in a variety of questions due to the poor record of the group, especially outside of South America.

facts.statement: A major issue with the North American dispersal hypothesis is the complete absence of sebecid material in continental North America, with only a ziphodont tooth from Cuba as potential evidence.
facts.quote: However a major issue with this hypothesis is the complete absence of any sebecid material in continental North America, with the only potential material being a ziphodont tooth from Cuba.

facts.statement: If not from European ancestors or North America, it is possible that Paleogene sebecids of Europe immigrated through Africa.
facts.quote: If not coming from European ancestors or via an unrecorded dispersal via North America, then the possibility arises that the Paleogene sebecids of Europe may have immigrated through Africa.

facts.statement: Following the discovery of Dentaneosuchus, Martin and colleagues proposed two additional models for the evolution of sebecids.
facts.quote: Martin and colleagues further consider the origin of sebecids as a whole following the discovery of Dentaneosuchus, proposing two additional models for their evolution.

facts.statement: One hypothesis suggests sebecids originated in Europe, dispersed into Africa, and rafted across the Atlantic to South America.
facts.quote: The first suggests not a Gondwanan origin for the family, but one centered in Europe, dispersing into Africa and rafting across the Atlantic to South America in a fashion similar to caviomorph rodents.

facts.statement: Another hypothesis suggests sebecids originated in Africa and dispersed independently into Europe and South America.
facts.quote: Another possibility raised by them is that sebecids originated in Africa and from there dispersed independently into Europe and South America.

facts.statement: These alternative origin models for sebecids run contrary to the traditional interpretation that they are of South American origin and require better fossil material to test.
facts.quote: Both ideas run contrary to the traditional interpretation that sebecids are of South American origin and would require further testing and most importantly better fossil material.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus exhibited massive size, matching the increase in size seen in contemporary European mammal species.
facts.quote: The massive size of Dentaneosuchus matches the increase in size undergone by contemporary mammal species of Europe.

facts.statement: Although the precise prey of Dentaneosuchus is unknown, its great size indicates it was an apex predator in its environment.
facts.quote: While the precise details of which prey Dentaneosuchus preferred are not known and require isotopic analysis to determine, the great size alone is a good indicator for the fact that this sebecid was an apex predator in its environment.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus could likely prey on animals its own size or larger, such as the early perissodactyl Lophiodon lautricense, which weighed up to 2,000 kg.
facts.quote: Dentaneosuchus would have likely been capable of preying on animals its own size and possibly larger. This includes the early perissodactyl Lophiodon lautricense, which could reach a weight of up to 2.000 kg and was found in the same deposits as the sebecid.

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus belongs to the parent group Sebecoidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Sebecoidea

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.quote: Type species: Dentaneosuchus crassiproratus

facts.statement: Dentaneosuchus lived from the Ypresian to the Bartonian, between 56 and 37.71 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Bartonian (56 to 37.71 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are two recorded fossil occurrences of Dentaneosuchus.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 2
